Jazz Oral History Project Interview with Al Hall Cassette 1-2
Interviewed by Ira Gitler
November 11, 1978
PRO-TYPISTS, INC. PROFESSIONAL TRANSCRIPTION SERVICE AREA CODE 202 347-5395
PROCEEDINGS
We're going to begin with the beginning. You're Alfred Wesley Hall. Where did the Wesley come from?
Well, Wesley was a Methodist name, most black families use Wesley.
If they're Methodist.
(Inaudible) mostly Methodist.
What about Baptists.
No, I don't know about that. Mostly Methodist.
And you were born, I see, in Jacksonville, Florida?
Right.
March the 8th, 1915. And it says raised in Philadelphia. Now, how long were you in Jacksonville and where were you between there and Philadelphia?
My family moved from Jacksonville when I was age two.
So you don't remember too much about it?

No, not too much about it. But that was during World War I and they were recruiting blacks to man the mills and what not. So we landed in Wilmington, Delaware before coming to Philadelphia. So I guess I was in Philadelphia about age five.
How many brothers and sisters?
I'm the only one.
Only child?
Yeah.
And were either of your parents musical?
No. My aunt taught me music. I started out piano about age seven. But --
Which aunt was this, on your father's or your mother's --
On my mother's side. Aunt Marie (PHONETIC).
Marie who?
Gilchrist.
So she began teaching you piano?
She began teaching me piano and -- but I wanted to be a violinist. So on my eighth birthday my parents bought me a violin and I had my first violin lesson when I was eight.
What inspired you to be a violinist?
We always had music in church and my first teacher, who taught me improperly, one of these who teach trumpet and voice and violin and whatnot, and I liked the violin.
You just liked the sound of it?
I liked the sound of the violin, yes. And so on my eighth birthday I began my musical career.
At the same time did you continue to study piano at all?
Up until about age 14, and I realized that I was being taught improperly on the violin, this way when (demonstrating) I should have been this way (laughing). You can't see that on the tape.
No. Crooking your hand?
Yeah. So I was in the junior high school orchestra and I changed violin teachers and he wasn't happy with my progress and he threatened to take me out of the school orchestra.
Where was this, in Philadelphia?
All of this is in Philadelphia.
What junior high school was this?
Shoemaker Junior High in Philadelphia, which was one of the first progressive junior high schools in that era, '30, these are the thirties. Circa twenties, really.

And then I had to give up the piano. I had to make a choice whether I was going to klutz around with the piano or learn how to play violin. He was an exceptionally fine violinist. In fact, he was one of the first blacks to get into Curtis Institute.
What was his name?
Leon Wisdom (PHONETIC). But he was very
light complexioned completed so --
That helped him.
Yeah, he only got in there on ability.
I know that was the very renowned school.
Right. (Break)
So here you are in the junior high school orchestra and you're still playing violin?
Uh-huh.
And at this time what were you listening to, as far as music?
I was strictly classical. Philadelphia was a classical town, supported by Curtis --
Institute, right.
And the Philadelphia Orchestra, with Stokowski (PHONETIC). So there were various clubs that an aspiring classical musician could ply his trade. (Inaudible).
What type of places?
Well, the Pine and Street Symphony Club (PHONETIC), various -- many. 200 members, what not.
They would have recitals and things?
No. Just rehearsals, play music. Played music. And the music changed. Met about two or three times a week.
Was that the one you belonged to, the
Pine Street?
Yeah.
Was it mixed, was it black or white or
No, it was all white.
You were one of the few black people involved?
Yeah. The only restriction was that you if missed three consecutive rehearsals, you were out. But I joined this as a bassist when I first started playing bass.
When did you switch to bass?
At age 17.
Then you were in high school?
High school.
What high school was this?
Overbrook High School. We had the best symphony orchestra in the city.
Had you stopped violin by this time?
No, I played violin and cello, bass, tuba.
In other words, it was just a natural evolution from the violin to the cello and the string bass?
Well, I was promoted from first stand band, second violin to the last stand, first violin.
This was after you got out of Shoemaker Schumacher and into Overbrook?
This is Overbrook. And the second violin

always played the afterbeats. The first violins were the virtu- osos. But when I got promoted to the last of the first violin, I was next to the bass. And our conductor was also our harmony teacher. And the two basses were going to graduate at the end of the term and so they needed some bass players. He asked for volunteers and I volunteered.
Cello came afterwards, then?
Cello came in later years.
Of course, the tuba was taught in place of the string bass in a lot of the bands, right? In the jazz bands.
In the jazz bands. I hadn't gone jazz, yet.
Yeah, I'm saying -- but you got to the tuba through the string bass, then?
No. The other way around. I went from the violin to the cello to the bass. I went from violin to bass to cello to bass, then tuba. (Inaudible) that comes later.
Yeah, but you got to the tuba, really, through playing bass, in a way?
Well, yeah, I guess so.
That was my point.
Okay, sorry.
So you were still in high school and you're still symphony, and you're playing bass?
Right.
: In the orchestra?
Uh-huh.
: And meanwhile, are you keeping up your association with the Pine Street Club?
Well, that's when I was -- yes, when I was bass player.
: Oh, when you were bass player you started to play.
So I'm with it and I said, you know, you missed three rehearsals of the Pine Street, you were out. Well, this was when I first started getting calls for the jazz bands.
: How did that happen?

Well, they heard that I had a string bass. They called and they came and picked me up, picked me up in, what do you call them, the Ford with the rumble seat. I didn't have a cover [for the bass] and I was using the school bass. And we went and rehearsed with a band for about a year before I even thought about being a professional jazz -- and we had such an odd combination, sousaphone, trumpet, two violin, and piano, drums. It was horrible.
(Laughter.)

"Lady Play Your Mandolin" was the popular song then. But when I first started the bass in 1932, the school would let me bring the bass home. And I'd come home and turn on the radio station and Louis Armstrong was on with "Sleepy Time Down South" and "Mississippi Mud," so I tried to play along with the
band. I guess that was Pops Foster.
Had you been interested in popular music and jazz before this?
I didn't have any direction at that point. I didn't know where I was going.
Because it was, you know, pretty available on the radio.
It was available on the radio but this was far-reaching in my mind, a full-time musician in Philadelphia was unheard of. You had to have a day job.
But the fact that you were playing mostly classical music --
Well, that was a dead end. I knew I wasn't going to go anywhere with that.
When did you realize this, in high school?

In high school. George Ockner (PHONETIC), a dear friend, I've got him on an album, was one of the finest violinists and at age 13 he was a child virtuoso with Stokowsky at the Philadelphia Orchestra. Okay, he was the leader -- he was at the first stand of violins when I got promoted -- first violin when I got promoted to the last band, first violin. And he auditioned for the Curtis Institute and got it. And I didn't have that opportunity.
So then I knew that violin wasn't going to be it.
I didn't know which direction bass was going to take me, either. It was just something to do.
Right. What were you thinking about as far as earning a living?
That hadn't come up, you know. I was still living with my family.
You didn't have to worry about that?
No.
And your father was working?
Yeah, Dad was a fine cement finisher.

All right. Now we're -- we were talking about, you know, your father was a cement finisher. So you really didn't have to worry about working. Then in this period when they came to get you and you started playing with this band, you were making gigs with them, huh?
Oh, no.
Just rehearsing?
We were just rehearsing.
Oh, that's right, you said that before. Okay. And what year was this, would you say?
1932. When I first got the bass.
Right. And then you started playing along with things on the radio and then you began to becoming aware of --
Jazz, yeah.
Would you say -- you know, you mentioned Louis, would you say that Louis was very important in drawing you into the music?

Louis, Bessie Smith, the local radio shops used to pipe the music out into the street and you'd hear these blues. Well, blues was a no-no in a middle class black family. That was sinful music. But it appealed to me.
Just to backtrack a little, were any of the musicians who you rehearsed with in that band, did any of them go on to play professionally, make any kind of a mark?
No. Like I said, that was unheard of in Philadelphia, to make music as a --

Yeah. All right, when you started playing, playing along with the radio and getting into jazz, did you then discover some other musicians in Philadelphia who you could play with who were into playing jazz?
Oh, well, then at the theaters, the Pearl Theater, the Lincoln Theater, all the musicians came from New York. So naturally I was always backstage.
Hanging out, uh-huh. Who were some of the first musicians you remember meeting?
Vic Dickenson, when he was with Blanche Calloway. When I was in high school, Wilson Meyers was the bass player with -- was the guitarist with the Seven
Spirits of Rhythm.
With the Seven Spirits of Rhythm?
Yeah.
Serious Meyers, huh?
Yeah, Serious Meyers, yeah. And they had had a radio broadcast in New York. And I just started playing bass with Willy Bryant's band, so he called me to fill in for him while he went to New York.
Oh, Willy Bryant was in Philly?

Willy Bryant was at the Lincoln Theater. In Philly. And Serious didn't come back until payday, and he came back on payday, got the pay and came back to New York. So he didn't play much. That's a little further along, as to how I got where I was in New York.
Well, according to the Encyclopedia here, you played with local bands from 1933 until 1935. What kinds of bands were those?

We had the best bands in Philly. Jimmy Shine's Jungle Band, you know, had those odd names. Les Robinson's band, which was the band that I -- the last band that I played with, [1936] 1935. Bessie Smith, that was her last engagement before she went South and got in the automobile accident.
Les Robinson's Band?
Yeah, at the Club Harlem.
Hall's correction
In Philly. Now, Les Robinson played what?
Drums.
Must have been a few Les Robinsons, over the years.
Les Robinson and Ted Tinsley (PHONETIC) was trumpets, Al Moore was the pianist then. He's a bass player now; he's with the Do Re Mi Trio.
Al Moore Miller?
Al Moore. Carl Wade (PHONETIC) had been a reject from the Lungeford Band in Buffalo. And I can't recall the rest of the guys. I was the only one in the band that could read music.
(Laughter.)
I was going to school at the time.
Where were you going then?

I was going to Masbaum (PHONETIC) Music School after I left Overbrook. This is when I took up the cello. And when Cab Calloway and Duke Ellington's band came into town, the only club -- they would come to the Club Harlem and we would play their hit songs. (Laughter). "Minnie the Moocher" for Cab and what was Duke's -- "Ring Them Bells", you know. We really didn't give a damn about them.
Did they sit in? Did anybody --
Oh, no, no. They just came to listen.

And we knew what band was coming into the theaters so we would create their hit songs when they came into town. And while -- oh, geez, I'm leaving out a very important factor. When I was a violinist, Billy Kyle was my accompanist. And we used to play social events, play all these (humming), you know.
(Laughter.)
But he left and went to Syracuse and then to New York, Billy Kyle. He was very talented. That was my first association of getting away from the classical aspects of playing.
What, playing with Billy Kyle?
Yeah. Because then I followed his career as he went to Syracuse, then to New York.
Now, was this at the same time as playing at the Club Harlem or right before?
No, this is before the Club Harlem. This is before I became a bass player. I was a violinist.
You played the violin, Kyle on piano, doing duos? (inaudible)?
Yeah, we used to play black society things, teas they called them, on a Sunday afternoon.
Tea dances.
(Laughter.)
What kind of tunes would you play?
Like I said, "Reve Evangelique," all classical
i.e. 'Meditation' from Thais (Massenet)
things, what a violinist would play, "Thais", those things, you know.
"Melody in F" and things like that?
Yeah, those sort of things.
"Lieberstraum"?
"Lieberstraum", by all means, that was a must.
(Laughter.)
Now, where does the tuba come in?

The tuba came in when I went to Masbaum after Overbrook. And Masbaum was a school, Jules Masbaum was a philanthropist in Philadelphia who also promoted jazz music, like the Curtis family. That's why they named the school after him. And it was a vocational school but it was the first vocational school that had introduced music. And the director of that school, Jules Levine, was a graduate of Temple University, which had the college music, grade A thing in Philadelphia. So he was conductor of the Masbaum Orchestra which was also -- superceded Overbrook Orchestra.
And of course Masbaum, over the years has turned out a lot of well-known musicians.
Oh, yeah, Joe Wilder and a lot of guys in music. Everybody went to Masbaum.
If they were given to play music?
Yeah. And that was also an audition

set-up, you had to play in order to get in. So the fact that I had already graduated high school, and this was a vocational school, I didn't have to take the academic subjects that the vocational school was affording. And we had music all day, from orchestra in the morning, concert, classical, you had to play another instrument than the one that you were accepted on. And then you had a choice of another instrument that they brought in professionals during the day, for their whole roster.
So you started on cello there?
That's when I took the cello.
And then you had tuba?
And the tuba.
That was the other instrument?

Yeah -- the cello was the other instrument. The tuba was something else to do. Because we had music all day. I have -- at a later time I have a roster that I can show you, the schedule. But it was music all day.
How about arranging? Did you have that.
Well, I was a harmony player, from high school, too.
At Overbrook. And then --
Yeah.
Okay, so then you were really getting into it.

I was getting into it and I didn't know I was into it, I'll put it that way. It was something to do and I was living at home and I didn't have to support myself. So that was available and I took advantage of it.
That was when -- that was concurrent with working with the bands, right? Because if Overbrook was '32 and then Massbaum was after that, you were then --
Well, it was at Massbaum that I really got into the jazz.
Yeah, and then you started playing --
Because I could bring the instruments home, I could bring the tuba home, bring bass home. I still didn't own a fiddle of my own, yet.
You were playing -- you said you were playing with these bands, at the Club Harlem --
That's afterwards.
But were you playing tuba as well as bass?

They wouldn't let me play tuba. I was the youngest bass player in Philly so I replaced the tuba player. They were getting away from that because the New York bands were coming in with string bass players.
Well, from the time you really got into it, you never, I guess, played the tuba --
Jazzwise? No. No.
What was Bessie like? What do you remember about that engagement?
Well, in retrospect I can't evaluate Bessie because she was just another blues singer at that time.
But you had been listening to her on records for a while before you played with her?
Oh, no, no. I caught her live performance. My family took me to a vaudeville show when she was the featured singer. But you must understand, this was sinful music.
Oh, I understand that. But you had said before you used to hear it coming out of the loudspeakers at the radio stores.
But it was Ethel Waters then, you know. She was the big name.
But Bessie had had many hits in the 20's, and yet you weren't listening to her.
But only the critics now have made Bessie superior to what Ethel Waters did.
Well, I'm not even talking about it from a critical standpoint, but, you know, she did sell a lot of records.
We weren't buying records then.
Well, who was buying those Bessie Smith records then?
Well, it certainly wasn't the blacks.
Maybe the blacks in the South were buying her records.
Maybe. Maybe.
But not so much in -- as you said, in the middle class music was frowned upon?
That's right.
Well, Ethel Waters, of course, was a big stage star.
Right. She's also from Pennsylvania, too. Chester, Pennsylvania. Well, so was Marion Anderson. Marion Anderson was a choir singer in our church.
I remember being down in Washington as a kid, at cherry blossom time when the DAR wouldn't let her sing, remember that?
Constitution Hall.
Yeah, I remember that very well.

Well, she was a choir singer in our church and she was envied by all the rest of the choir members in our church because of her sensational voice. You couldn't evaluate then what you can now, as to what was happening. When you ask me about Bessie Smith, okay; there was Mamie Smith, there were a whole lot of other singers, you know. But they all sang the blues and you didn't know who was the best at that time.
So in other words, when you backed
her that time, she didn't impress you because she was late in her career then, and she hadn't been doing so well.
She was (unintelligible) then, anyhow. going downhill
Was she married to Jack Gee (PHONETIC) then?
I don't know.
He was the Philadelphia policeman --
I read the story later but I didn't know. We weren't into that. The kind of clubs that were in Philadelphia at that time, this is pre-Prohibition and after, and Pearl Bailey was a part of this --
She was?
But the performer would go out and entertain the people and collect tips. Hence, the kitty.
Go from table to table?
Go from table to table and get the tips, and then they'd come back and put it in the box and they'd split it with the band.

So now they're getting real smart, we're getting real smart, you know. People throw money out on the floor or during the Prohibition days if you had a saxophone or tuba you'd get some smart ass that would try to flip a silver dollar into your horn and all that, dent your horn. (Unintelligible) they paid but, you know. It's demeaning now but that was the thing. You know, throw money out on the floor and everybody
run and scramble and try to pick it up, you know, and all that sort of thing.

And Bessie was at the Club Harlem with Les Robinson. Les Robinson's group, and she'd go from table to table. And then they got a younger girl who tried to pick up coins off of, you know, with their snatches (inaudible), you know, stack of dimes or --
(Laughter.)
I heard about that when I went out to school in Missouri. Over in East St. Louis they used to play this, you know --
Oh, East St. Louis? Oh, wow, that's it.
That was the kind of story they told about East St. Louis. But now was the Club Harlem and after-hours kind of club?
Oh, no, no. Regular hours.
Yet they would have things going on like that?
That was the entertainment. That was the entertainment. (inaudible) you know. So it was all live entertainment. There weren't any juke boxes then, either,
What other things did they have in the show?
A dancer, comic.
Well, these girls used to walk around, using their snatches -- did they ever strip?
No, no, no. No, we didn't have that. That was a technique, you know, a stack of dimes or a stack of dollars, whatever (inaudible).
(Laughter.)
Pearl Bailey used to do it. That was a different kind of an act. Then you had a singer, an M.C., comedian --
Hopefully.
Yeah, hopefully, you know. This was the beginning of plying your trade in show business, you know.
Now, had you started doing any solos by then or did you just play in the ensemble? Or did you get solos?

Yeah, I got solos. One of the first solos that I ever did was Claude Hopkin's theme song, 'I Could do Almost Anything For You.' And I used to wear a big red hat and straddle and slap and spin. This was show biz. If you didn't do that -- and I was an up and coming bass player at that time.
Did you do bowing, too, on solos?
Oh, yeah --
On solos?
No. No.
Yeah, I knew you could bow. So when you took a solo you just slapped or picked?
Yeah, slapped.

Ride it like a horse?
Yeah, spin it. Wear a funny hat, you know. That was it. That was at the Club Harlem in 1934, with Bobby Booker's Orchestra -- (End of side 1 as recorded.)
We had a hell of an orchestra there. We stayed the whole season.
So you worked there with several different bands?
No, one band.
No, I mean then Les Robinson later.
This is after Les Robinson.
Oh, this is after Les Robinson.
Yeah.
What other bands were there?
Tiny Bradshaw.
When was this?

'34. We came to New York, we played the Lincoln Theater in Philly and then came to the Apollo, big band. Double on violin, we had three violins, we had vocals, we had a Fred Waring type thing that wasn't going anywhere.
(Laughter.)
Who was in that band that you remember?
Gee, I'd have to think about that.
But no one that continued, made some
No.
What about Tiny Bradshaw? Because he had bands for quite a while.
The less said about it the better.
(Laughter.)
All right. So was that your first trip to New York?

As a professional, yes. And we were underpaid. We came to the Apollo and Tiny had been slapped with a union fine, which we didn't know about. And we weren't going to go on until he paid up his fine. And he harrassed us because we were all squares from Philadelphia. Had a hell of a band, though, big band. Biggest band I've been in.
How many pieces?
Oh, close to 20.
(End of proceedings as recorded.)

Well, we have plenty of time, to talk about it, so if you think of something else later, don't hesitate to throw it in.
You said Tiny was the only vocalist but you said you had a Fred Waring type.
Well, we had three fiddles --
When you said Fred Waring, I thought of the Glee Club.
No, no, instrumentally.
I thought maybe some of the band were also singing as well. The ways bands used -- sometimes the whole band would sing in those days, you know.
No, we didn't have anybody sing --
At this time were you into jazz that much that you had your favorites and you had some bass players who you favored and who you were inspired by.
Not yet. I always inspired by John Kirby and Billy Taylor who was with Duke.
This was a little later, right.
Well, when I started playing bass, these were the people that I heard.
Did you hear Kirby when he was with Fletcher Henderson?
No, I didn't hear him when he was with

Fletcher, but he used to come to Philadelphia. He was with Fletcher Henderson, but I didn't get a chance to go hear the band because they were playing at a club but wherever I was playing, after they finished, you know the musicians, they'd come from New York and go to the various spots.
And I was always working in some little joint in Philly.

Now, you mentioned when Ellington or Calloway used to come to hear -- there was no sitting in but how about in these other kind of places. Was there jamming and sitting in or did you get a chance to...
No. The jamming didn't happen until New York. They didn't come -- they were finished with what they had to do.
They just came to relax and listen.
Yeah.
Okay. So you made the trip to New York with Tiny Bradshaw and you're back to Philly, and let's see that was '34 and then what happened?
'34. I guess the kind of run into one another We got some dates (unintelligible) because when I left Les Robinson at the Club Harlem I came to the Catskills.
When was this?
You went to the Catskill Mountains?
Yeah. Woodbourne.
How did you happen to go up there?
I got a wire, got a call.
What bands?

The rhythm section of the Erskine Hawkins band had been off and they were working there. Lowell Morgan [Staufield] who is still around, and the bass player's name, Lee and the drummer, and Erskine has a gig and so they have to come back and they need a replacement so Fathead Lawrence have to look that up too, he's a hell of a baritone, played without a strap.
Must have had some strong hands.

Terrific. He and I were called from Philadelphia to make the gig in Woodbourne. So we went to Woodbourne and the mountains weren't too populated at that point, so the gig closed before Labor Day, and we came back to New York. He was from Hampton, Virginia, he went to Virginia and I came to New York.
Who was that from Virginia?
Fathead Lawrence, and that's how I stayed in New York.
And this is 1936.
Yeah. I never went back to Philly.
What did you do, find an apartment or a hotel?

No, I stayed with the drummer that had replaced the drummer, Sam Clark -- I don't want to leave his name out, he's deceased. I stayed at his apartment and I made every rehearsal that was called upon. I was carrying my bass up and down 7th Avenue every day, because I was from Philly and a square and this is what we would have done in Philly.
You get to the rehearsal and it's supposed to be eight pieces and maybe six will show, you know, and so you got to call it off and carry my bass back and forth, so I went through that, too.
Who did you meet in that period of time.
Then I met everybody. Which will bring me to Serious Meyers (phonetic) he didn't pay me in Philadelphia. He came and collected the money and came right back to New York.
After you had subbed for him.
Yeah, and he was one of the first persons I met when I came to New York and he was rehearsing with Billy Hicks and his Sizzling Six, so he was too busy and he gave me the rehearsal.
Was that kind of a way of paying you back.
Paying me back.
I started it at the Savoy Ballroom. Bill Hicks got the gig at the Savoy Ballroom, opposite Chick Webb and we stayed a year and a half.
Now, I don't know too much about
that band. I have known the name, such a catchy, right, Billy Hicks and his Sizzling Six, but tell me something about that band.
Well, we had Edmund Hall, Fernando Arbello, Skippy Boland, Arnold Boland, Cyril Haynes, and forgot the guitarist's name. I'll get that. But we had the jumping band.
Let's see, trombone, clarinet and --
But it wasn't Dixieland. It was an arranged sort of thing.
Did Edmund double on anything or did he just play clarinet.
He just played clarinet. It was my first meeting Edmund. He had just left Claude Hopkins band, big band and we were there a year and a half, and this is the year that I joined the union.
What did Billy Hicks play.
Trumpet. He was a la Bix Bates. He didn't go too high, he didn't go too high, he was right in the middle, but he was fantastic. But then we had to wear funny hats and all that crap.
What kind of a book did you have, you said, it wasn't Dixieland.
Played the --
Played the songs of the day.
Yeah, we played the popular songs of the day. But they were more or less arranged, and we read and rehearsed which was unusual.
The drummer was who?
Arnold Boland, Scrippy Boland.
B-o-l-a-n-d.
B-o-l-a-n-d, I think.
Boland.
Arnold Boland. I can check that.
And Cyril Haines on the piano.

Well, Cyril Haynes was the followup pianist for -- we had a pianist that was a real nut. I can't think of his name, and Cyril followed him and then when the Savoy Sultans followed us, Cyril was with them, because he was playing gigs at that point. Ram was a famous pianist at that point.
Ram Ramirez.
Yes. Eddie Haywood, Teddy Wilson, they were the favorite pianists. Edgar Hayes. Clyde Hart. Billy Kyle hadn't come yet to New York.
Now, you were saying before when we were talking about the way the big band would stop and your band would take off, what was that.
Whatever tune they played, we would
pick it up.
Did this ever make them mad or did they feel you were trying to outdo them or was it always the spirit of competition.

This was a period of appreciation of what somebody else did. This new phase of people being envious of one another playing their instruments, that wasn't in existence then. A guy in the band or on a bandstand that played a beautiful solo, his fellow musicians would give him the accolade he deserved, you know.

Then they had a period of superior talent like when -- they say of the Duke Ellington band, the guys would turn their backs -- I am not going to name any names because they're all friends of mine, but they'd turn their backs on a fellow soloist because I am the great "I am." That's a later development of the jazz scene, and during the period of my coming up under that scene, if a guy played a beautiful solo, you told him. And the next time he played the solo, he'd play it better, and you'd feel better, you know. But everybody became a specialist, and it became an envy thing.
When do you think that started happening?
I'd say in the fifties, because in the rock and roll scene, I made all of those, teenagers, the Meltones, the So and So tones, these tones, Al Freed.

In '46, and --

Yeah.

Oh, at the Watts Club.
I left there and went --

With Eddie Condon and toured with Cliff Jackson, one of the most wonderful tours I ever had. What was the name of the singer?
(Inaudible). Lee Wiley?
(Inaudible) and her husband,
now I can get the names, - Jess Stacey (phonetic), Ernie Cacerfas, Bobby Hackett, Joe Thomas.

Well, I had been working with Eddie down in the Village. When I was substituting for Sid Weiss or Jack either Lesberg or somebody.

In '46 when they --
Opened his club? So, you've been with all kinds of, you know, styles in the music.
Without being egotistical, I can say I have covered the field.
Right.
From the symphonies, I did the Ballet USA in '58, and symphonic and jazz.

Right. One of my first recordings was with Woodie Guthrie.

Right.
Playing one-string (inaudible) fiddle. And Josh White --

Yeah. Mary Lou Williams.
Yeah, you are with Bill Coleman.
Yeah, that was the trio.
Same prize Surprise records, some of the first records I bought personally.
Really?
Yeah, I told you my brother had --
Yeah.
Gone to the Navy and among the first records I bought, that was among the first records I bought.

Yeah, that was quite a ball. Bill and I had been working with Ellis Larkins at this point and Ellis burned his fingers lighting a cigarette, the match went off in his hands, so Mary Lou Williams finished out the engagement at Cafe Society Uptown --
And that's how --
And during that time, the record date came about. That's how Bill and I were with Mary Lou.
But, you know, Condon was probably one of the few of the so-called white Dixieland or Chicago musicians in those days, musicians who did mix the bands black and white.
Not too much. He was pretty --
But more than a lot. Most of them were either black bands or white bands, especially in Dixieland, became, as you said before, white music.
Right.
And Condon always did have some kind of a mixed band. He had Edmund Hall, Hot Lips Page.
Well, that -- that came in later years. Yeah. But it was restricted to those few that you named, you know, John Doe couldn't come in.
Yeah. Well, the point is though, that however restricted, it was, that was unique in itself, you know.
Right.
Because none of the other guys that played that kind of music did use black musicians at all. That's why I brought it up thinking, you know, it was something.
Well, Eddie had a big band at one time that we played against when I was with Teddy Wilson's big band in New England. We watched 'em away. Bobby Hackett had a big band at one time too.
That I heard. It ran the gamut.
Oh? But, yeah, I guess Eddie did it before, I don't know, no, he didn't do it before Benny Goodman or Artie Shaw.
No, no. And at the time he did it, it

was already more common. (Blank) was doing it by that time, it had become more commonplace in the modern groups, you know, and Bird and Stan Levy and Dizzy and Al Haig and people like this, it seemed to be a more natural thing with the modern groups like it just happened. Because these guys who could play this kind of music gravitated you know, together.
Well, no, it didn't just happen. When you say, Stan Levy and Diz --
Well, they were from Philly.
But they are already in New York now.
Yeah, but they knew each other from Philly.
Yeah, but they weren't working that much.
Yeah.
You see Eddie was at Jimmy Ryan's and they had an established group after Louis Prima.
Also, didn't they used to have sessions at Ryan's on Sunday and that was --[white]
That's when it became --
To be mixed, yeah.

Right, yeah. But when you say Diz and Stan Levy, this is much later. So, you know, it didn't matter who was on the bandstand as long as they could play, but the Dixieland thing was pretty much a closed shop. You had Joe Thomas, Edmund Hall, Walter Page. I followed Walter Page at

the Downtown when he got arthritis in his fingers and couldn't play and then when I left, I gave it to Leonard Gaskin (inaudible), but Eddie was more Waspish in his thinking than you think he -- he had some friends. (sentence inaudible). I don't know how to come out of that.
I'm still, you know, we are talking about this whole period in general because you were doing so many things. All right, you came off the tour with him and that's when you went into 'Barefoot Boy.'
Not exactly. I came off the tour on November 1st, when my youngest daughter was born and 'Barefoot Boy' started in March.
Of '47. So, what did you, did you just played around --
Yeah.
Around town?
Yeah, gigs.

Yeah.

I don't know. It has been put out in album form.

In Sweden.
In Europe, yeah. No one has put it out here?

I don't know.
You don't know. I wonder who does?

Well, where is she?

Becomes public domain. It is on a label called Crystal, have you seen it?
No. We'll look at it later.
All right.

Yeah, well, I played in shows up until this last year. I substitute in shows and sub in theaters. I've been invited to come to 'The Wiz' which will close pretty soon. But Mr. (inaudible) is going to try to get another company
to go out on the road. Arvell Shaw is doing it.
So then, what else were you doing then --
In the '40's?
No, yeah, in the '40's and into the you know, early '50's, you were still obviously working in the shows.
I was still doing the shows. I was in shows and then I worked with Pearl Bailey. The Louie Belson band worked with Don Redman (inaudible). We traveled a little bit.
When was this?
Then before that, you mentioned you were with Count Basie's band?
Yeah, and what was that? Was that when he, before he put the band back together again?
No.
Because he had the small group for a couple of years there.
This was just before he recorded the hit --
Every Day?

"Every Day". But I had been with Errol Garner then. I made Errol Garner's "Misty" (inaudible). I was working there. Oh, in the '50's, I was working with Errol. Hazel Scott, '53, '53 I was with Errol GARNER.
How long were you with him?
Six months.
What was that like?

I worked with him later, too. Osie (inaudible) Johnson and I, we made the Other Voices album. And I played with the Cleveland Symphony. (Laughter) My wife has was asked whether a musician has an orgasm when he's playing. This was it. This was it. I couldn't identify it as such. 7,000 people and all of these ten bass players, cut them out. Just me, right in the middle of the string section. Boy Wow. I was on cloud nine.
What year was this?
I'd have to check it out. It was Sometime in the '50's.
Some time in the '50's.
Yeah. Yeah.

Clubs.
Clubs at that time.

Yeah.

In the whole evolution of bass playing, who do you see as the important, you know, players who really, you know, changed the bass and opened it up?

Jimmy Blanton changed the bass. Jimmy Blanton changed the whole concept of the bass. But I think the greatest bass player that I know is Ray Brown. He is complete in all aspects. I'm not putting down anybody else, but Ray Brown is --
How about Pettiford?

Oh, Pettiford was a copist of Jimmy Blanton. Well, he was a performer. He couldn't read too well which, you know, would keep him away from -- this is the difference in when I came up, coming out of a symphony orchestra, I could read. I'm always a bridesmaid, never a bride. (Laughter) But, Pettiford started his
career copying Jimmy Blanton. Ray Brown copied Blanton but he had enough other things going for him that he developed it beyond --

Well, listening to Pettiford, especially when he played the cello, you know, and improvised, his line sounded a lot like stuff that Charlie, you know, that he had listened pretty hard to Charlie Christian.
Well, we all did.
Yeah.

Yeah, yeah. Charlie Christian. Blanton, They just lived too fast. Charlie Christian, they were young musicians, genius. But, who's we used to say that what they contributed, that they could have contributed more -- Jimmy Blanton died at 22, Charlie Christian died about 24.
And yet they had such an impact in those short --
They left their trademark, so, if they had lived say, up until now, what else could they have done?
Well, as far as innovation, maybe not, but they would just have become, you know, more mature in their own style.
Yeah.
But they, you know, they have that whole question about in classical music it seems that, Horowitz (inaudible) or Rubenstein, whatever is revered or appreciated you know, as

they grow into later years. In jazz, people are looking for the newest thing instead of appreciating what you can still do, maybe it isn't, you know, those people are not innovating in classical music.
No.
But a jazz musician is expected to do something new all the time instead of appreciating him for the, you know, the depths that come with age and, you know, just continuing to -- for excellence.
Right, right.
Why do you think this is, there are these two sets of standards?

Well, there again, it comes up to polarization because classical music is basically European and jazz, ad-lib music, I'd rather used that word than (inaudible) jazz black oriented and undisciplined. I think that's a better word for it, even on both sides of the fence. I remember practicing my violin and my bass and the same notes that never changed. Nobody can write the notes that you play on the bandstand.

Until black musicians started reading more, learning harmony and what not. more a guy would play a solo and an astute arranger could copy down what he was playing and show it to him and he wouldn't be able to touch it. (Laughter)
Yeah.
Really? Did I play this?
By the same, you know, meaning, you could notate it and yet, if someone else tried to play it, it wouldn't sound at all --
Right, right.
But maybe the musician who played it could because he would play it with the same --
No --
But he couldn't even duplicate it.
The musician that played it would recognize it as such, as being notated. Yeah, a student could learn it. He wouldn't get the feeling of it.
Well, what about some other bassists who you would come into contact with over the years who perhaps didn't get credit for what they did? Could you, you know, would any come to mind?
Well, I think all the bassists that are credited are, have already reached --

No, we know the Bill Hinton's and the George Diviveas (phonetic) you know, people such as this who made reputations and have been playing for years and years and are still playing. I was just, you know, asking about maybe someone that we don't know about.
No, I think if he did you would know about it, unlike some trumpet players or saxophone players or whatnot, but, there are not many bass players that are
worth their salt that you don't know about.
Why do you think that's true?

Well, first of all, the rhythm section, you know, always has to prevail you know, you don't have anything else going for you without a rhythm section, so, the guys could play are the guys that you know about. The guys that can't play -- unlike a Taft Jordan or a Dick Vance, these are master musicians you know. Although Taft can't play anymore. [es of 1978 due to surgery on his jaw]
Yeah.
But, there are multiple instruments that are more or less in a section rather than being individual, as a drummer, bass, piano. But, the bass player that can play everybody knows about.
Yeah, well, it seems that bass players and drummers are always in demand, always looking for -- because usually the good ones are doing something.
Right, right..
When did you play with Ellington?

I played for Ellington in the '70's. at the Rainbow Grill When Joe Benjamin got injured. Two times he got injured. I was standby for the Soviet trip but Ellington took too many people in his entourage, that I was left behind. But I was supposed to go.
All right, so we see from --
That was Ellington.
Yeah. From the period of when you
started playing in the show bands, in the pit bands, this continued until very recently. That was more or less your mainstay and you worked around that?
Yes. I did about fifty shows, or more.
Well, here is the Jerome Robbins Ballet USA you were talking about, in '58?
Yeah.
And Yves Montand in '59.
Twice I worked (inaudible) for him.
Yeah.
He came back, we toured Canada, California. In fact, I was working with Yves Montand the day that Ernie --
Kovacks?
Ernie Kovacks got killed. He was supposed to come back in the car with him.

So, now, around this revolved gigs, you know, over a long period of time. What were, you know, some of the more memorable associations that you have had in that period which spans, you know, the last 20 years. We are talking about, you know, 25 years ago.

Well, I think the Errol Garner symphony was one of my more, that I can remember mostly, and I made an initial album with Victor Borge when he first came from with Paul Barry's orchestra Europe, and there were two basses and I was made the first We played some Brahms; "All the Things You Are" and Casper Reardon bass, 60 strings playing, (inaudible), and Mitch Miller was
oboeist. He was the world's greatest at the time. (inaudible). These are the things I think about.
Yeah.
Jazz wise, I don't know anything that would stand out. I made a concert with, I was a contractor of Carnegie with the All Blues session (inaudible) That was my first date on Fender bass.
Which blues session was this?
What's the popular --
B. B. King?
Yeah, yeah, and we had the first half of the program.

No, just a concert at Carnegie. And Elvin Jones was the leader of the group and I got the musicians, had Lawrence Lucie on guitar, Russ Andrews on tenor and Wynton Kelly on piano and everybody said 'wow,' I mean, how do you get these guys to play the blues and our opening singer was Joe Turner, and we had wall to wall people and our first note — we didn't give a damn whether B. B. King came on or not. (Laughter) I love him, now, don't get me wrong.
Right.
But we had a swinging group. And I can't get that record. It was on The Flying Dutchman, with Bob Thiele.
Now, looking over your, you know,
your list of credits, you recorded with Johnny Hodges.
Yeah, "Back to Back", "Side By Side".
And Billy Holiday?
Yeah.
When did you --
"Practice Makes Perfect" and "Same Old Story", that was in --
In the period of all those great recordings?

Yeah, it was in, that was about '40, 1940, or '41. That's the only date I did with her.. Don Redman was the leader of the band with Jimmy Hamilton and George (inaudible) and Don Byas and J. C. Herd, Roy Eldrige.
Yeah, well, I mean, it was amazing to me, you know, in listening to those records all the time the amount of talent that went through, you know, and there was so much talent around. In that period.
Yeah.

And you know, this is something that has been said before, but it's still a truism, that there were so many people playing in that era who were talented, and yet they may have been, you know, working in similar styles but everyone sounded different, everyone had their own little thing. Why do you think there was that much variety?
Well, we hadn't gotten into electronics

yet. So a guy had his own identity. This is what I try to teach my pupils of using the amplifier. For the bass, you got an Fender amplifier and you've got your music to read, John Doe can play it and he'll sound, he'll play the song but he won't have any identity. But when you play your instrument and I teach with gut strings instead of steel strings, but you got your personal feeling to it.
Yeah.
And I can tell who is playing the bass on anything, the bass instrument rather than the fender, but I couldn't identify who would be playing the fender bass.
Right, it's the same thing with the electric piano, it makes --
Right, right.
-- it makes, reduces you to just a faceless --
Yeah, you are a plug in the wall. Pull the plug out or the fuse goes and you are out, you are out of business. It's happened. Or electrocuted, which is worse. (Laughter)
You know, but, even more than that like, say, on the saxophone, there were just so many people that came say, out of Hawkins, who, but they were all their own men.
Right.
Whereas --
Including Ben.
Oh, Ben, and Don Byas and -- there were so many of them, but, Herschel Evans. Everybody had their own, it was like a speaking voice.
Right. Right.
You knew who it was as soon as you heard it, but in the post-Coltrane era, we've had like so many saxophone players who were just trying to play like Coltrane and they all sound alike.
Right. Right.

And now I'll say, I'm not going to name any names, but there were some established players who did have their own, you know, particular vocabulary and sound who went over and ended up sounding not like anything but a Coltrane clone.
Right. Right.
Which has nothing to do with electronics.
No, but that was desperation. That was trying to get a job. Jazz-wise what you asked me last year. I did the Bob Crosby Bobcats on the Rotterdam cruise.
Oh, yeah, you were telling me.
So, naturally, I'm supposed to whistle Big Noise from Winnetka.
Oh, God.
The day before I lost a tooth. (Laughter)
That's fantastic.
But I did it.
Yeah.
I did it.
How did you become a Bobcat so late in life?
They called me.
Just like that.
Yeah, I live by the telephone.
You know, it's interesting because of your -- so many associations with show business and shows, like, you seem to have done a lot of work with singers and you know, personalities.
Well, I consider myself an accompanist from the early days in Philadelphia on up. This is how I was raised.
Who was accompanying who with Billy Kyle? You were complimenting each other.
Oh, I'm not, not the violin days.
I know, I know, I'm just --
But --

Once I started playing bass this is all we did, you know. This was the dance era so a bass solo would throw the dancers off meter.

But the difference between being a symphony player and being a person to play ad lib was that the symphony player was disciplined bar by bar to make this B flat, and it was an impersonal B flat. I'm just using B flat as a note, because my star pupil, Mike Slattery, I used to give him hell about B flat, so he calls himself B flat Mike.
(Laughter.)

But the notes themselves has a lot to do with the people that surround an ad lib player more than the discipline of a symphony player. And this is how you create a lifestyle, as to how you play. Uh-huh. And you can come into the club and be influenced by the atmosphere and the people.
Of the people that are there.
People who you're working for?
Right.
And people who you're working with.
Right.
And the people who come to hear you?

Right. You have a whole scope of things that are going through -- unconsciously going through your mind. You can -- all of these factors have a bearing on what you're playing, and you can still be worrying about paying the rent.
(Laughter.)
You know, whether you're going to get paid that day or not. Any of those things.
But family life has a lot to do with it. I came from a very disciplined family, so my playing is disciplined. I feel miserable if I make a mistake, sound bad, you know, to myself.
Well, you often think musicians are harder on themselves than anyone else because --
Yes.

-- I mean as a professional listener myself who doesn't always listen as a critic, can, you know, listen for enjoyment. I'll go up to a musician and say, you know, sincerely you really played beautifully tonight, and they'll say, no, I wasn't really getting it, you know, and I can, you know, not up to my own expectations.

Right. Well, not only that, you hear things that the listener isn't even aware of, maybe the tempo, length of the note or the sound of the note or anything, you know, that you're well aware of. All of you -- well, like I said, your instrument is an extension of yourself. So what it means is that you've got this impersonal instrument that you have got to make say something, and you're listening to yourself, not amplified, but another appendage-like. I don't know if I'm explaining that to you.

Well, I understand it. And the pianist has the hardest job in a way because sometimes the instruments he's given to work on or work with are inferior; whereas usually the other instruments are -- the personal property of the musicians, and they care for them in such a way that, you know, they usually perform, although there are always technical breakdowns with your, you know, with your own instruments, because they're only manmade tools.
Well, I don't -- I don't give piano a priority on being that difficult because it's a fixed instrument.

Like it's a guitar almost sometimes.

fact that a lot of the musicians who came out of that era, you know, decided they weren't going to be Uncle Toms, you know, and they were going to go straight ahead as people. Six weeks, uh-huh.

Yes, uh-huh. So we've been doing that at --
Red Blazer.

-- at the Red Blazer. Then I've worked at Red Blazer on Saturdays with Bob Cantwell, and we have a group called the Saturday Night Stompers, Dixieland type thing. So if between those something else comes up, it makes a week, a weak week.
(Laughter and recording interruption.)

Addendum to Al Hall. A propos of the Bill Coleman and you leaving Teddy Wilson, I think -- I haven't listened to that part of the tape again, but you said you referred to the reason for your firing is that you were too international.
Right.
Would you elaborate on that?

Well, Barney Josephson's brother was in charge of the Cafe Society Uptown at the time, and when we left downtown Cafe Society to go Uptown to open it, we opened it. And we had certain restrictions that were posted on the bulletin board, and one of them was that we couldn't drink at the bar downstairs. So we had to go up four flights of stairs to our dressing room.
And a couple nights a couple customers came in -- Benny Goodman's brother, the bass player. Gee, I can't --
Harry.

Harry, Harry Goodman -- insisted on buying me a drink downstairs. Well, that caused a little disruption in THE attitudes there. Then a fellow from Belgium came over to see Bill Coleman, and I was working with the Golden Gate Quartet, and he was buying Bill a drink downstairs. This is no-no land. The bartenders can get fired if they serve us.

So we always had our own bottles upstairs anyhow, playing cards and, you know, take -- you know, you could relax, but it was still four flights upstairs, walking, uncomfortable quarters. So this fellow -- this fellow from Europe really admired Bill's work. And I was playing with the Golden Gate Quartet, which you could hear a pin drop. They

added a bass to the quartet, and I went on with the M- between sets, between our sets. And Bill had to go to the men's room, and he left his horn on the bar, and THIS ADMIRER picked it up and made a big blast -- toot.
(Laughter.)
So Bill was instantly fired.
Something he didn't --
He's at the Metro. He got fired, you know. So when we left -- when we left to go to Chicago at the Pump Room and Barney didn't want us to leave then because --
You mean he was fired, but he was rehired?
You mean Teddy Wilson?
No, no. Bill --
Oh, Bill? Yeah, he wasn't really fired. We would have had a trio, you know. But -- I lost my point.
When you left to go to the Pump Room --
Oh, yeah, we were in disfavor of the Cafe Societies then because we were breaking in a new territory for the William Morris Agency, MCAD [Music Corporation OF AMERICA]
Right, I think we did talk about this.
Yeah. Yeah.
But you were too international.
But we were inseparable, he and I, so we -- so when Teddy tried to get rehired there, he could get rehired minus us, you know. So we stand back for a long time -- negatives.
(Laughter.)
Now, to go back even farther, in reading what you had there on a sheet, you know, you talked about a Club Harlem in Atlantic City, which we didn't, I think, get into earlier.

Oh. The Club Harlem in Atlantic City was the Black nightclub happening, Cotton Club-wise, because they had chorus girls and comics and, well, it was the only nightclub that was established in Atlantic City, run by Mr. Williams, and I started my career basically there with Bobby Booker's band.
Well, where did you play with Bobby Booker's band in Philly?
I forgot the name of the place. I'll think of it, though. But we were the small Teddy Wilson type band, that type arrangements and --
At the Club Harlem in Atlantic City.
Yeah. Yeah.
And you were mentioning that you met quite a few people at that club.
Yeah, Leo Carillo and what's the name?
Helen Morgan.
Helen Morgan.
What was he doing with Helen Morgan?

They came in together and bought the band champagne, and she sang with us, yeah. All the movie stars used to come. Well, that was the hot spot in Atlantic City in the 1920s, the late '20s and the '30s. This was all (inaudible) still the place to go.

But it's -- it all points out to be a segregation sort of thing anyhow, you know, but the nightclub was downstairs, and the dance hall was upstairs. So you had bands like Lunceford and Chick Webb, and this is how I met Beverly Pier, Eubie Blake -- what was his partner's name?
Sissle?
Noble Sissle. Ed Cole was playing with Noble Sissle.
Nat Cole's brother?
Yes, he was a bass player. He was the smoothest, satiny-est bass player I ever saw, and I wanted to adapt my playing after him, along with John Kirby and Billy Taylor, Sr. That's my style.
Yeah, very smooth.
Yeah, because when I was -- when I was young and first started playing at 17, I saw Erskine Hawkins'
band come to the theater, and Stanfield was the bass player. And he was slapping and straddling and spinning it and whatnot.
Well, you had to do that too, you remember.
Well, that was the style.
What you were talking about before.
Yeah. So --
Wearing a big red hat, you said.
Yeah, a big red hat. This was at the Club Harlem, yeah, surely.
So you had to do that.
Yeah. So I was working with this band that I spoke about earlier at the Club Harlem in Philadelphia. Well, there were always Club Harlems everywhere. Let's face it.
(Laughter.)

And we were playing opposite Charlie Gaines' band in Philadelphia with the band that Louis Jordan was in. So the bass player's name was Mr. Hayes. I never remembered his first name, but I always remember he was Mr. Hayes. So he was like about 37, and I'm 17, you know, smart, you know.
He was an old dude.
And he used to sit back, and he was cool, he was cool too, like Eddie Cole, but not as polished as

Eddie Cole. So I get out on the floor and play Claude Hopkins's themesong, "I Could Do Almost Anything for You," and spin the bass and straddle it and slap it and wear the hat with the -- he said, "son, when you're spinning it, you're not playing it." And from that point on I stopped. And I tried --
Uh-huh. Art Blakey once told me that Chick Webb told him, "son, the music is on the drum, not in the air."
(Laughter.)
Art Blakey made -- I was on Art Blakey's first record date with Andy Kirk, had the band, and it was Billy Daniels' first recording for Decca. Yeah, Art Blakey -- Billy Kyle was the pianist.
You're old partners.
Yeah.
Now, you also mentioned to me that there are other people you left out that you want to talk about, including Stuff Smith.

Are we on now? Well, when you mention -- when -- Stuff Smith gave me an idea of all the violins that (inaudible) played with, starting from Woodie Guthrie on the one string fiddle for Asch Records, and I played with all the violinists that -- all the noted violinists through Eddie South and Joe Venuti and Ray Nance and --
How about Keller Grappelli? --
No, I never played -- I never met him. And I'm speaking about American violinists. And Charlie Dixon Jazz Accorde we mentioned, Jaja Bord, and I forget the violinist that's with Kansas City.
Oh, Williams, Fiddler? [Claude]
Yeah, yeah, but he wasn't a fiddler originally, was he? He was a guitarist.
He played guitar and fiddle.
Yeah. I worked Michael's club with them too. So I covered most of the fiddle players. And Stuff Smith was extra special because I was with him when my first born was born, you know, in Chicago.
Stuff Smith is probably the -- the most swinging of all the fiddle players, wouldn't you say?
Well, yeah, but there was a --
How about Ray Perry?

Ray Perry, yes, I've played with Ray. And there was a violinist in Philadelphia by the name of [Wesley] Robinson before I even heard of the rest of these fiddles. But I was a symphony violinist, and I never could play that on the violin, and I guess maybe that influenced my playing the bass. You know, I -- wouldn't have gone anywhere as a symphony violinist.
Yeah, but do you think you would have played jazz on the violin?
No, I couldn't. No, no, Lady, Play Your Mandolin was a popular tune then, you know, and this Robinson, and I can't think -- Wesley Robinson -- Wesley Robinson was a fiddle player in Philadelphia.
Was he related to that Les Robinson, the drummer?

No. No. He and Stuff Smith were neck and neck as far as playing jazz. We didn't have the outlets, the media to judge these sort of things. Neither did we have critics at the time to evaluate who was who -- who was better and, you know --
Yeah, and publicize it and all.

Yes. So one guy's in Buffalo. The other guy's in Philadelphia, but the music's all the same because the guy's are traveling, you know, troubadors, and so you take your craft with you, and other people get influenced by it. So the myth of New Orleans music being the jazz center of the world wasn't necessarily so.
Yeah, this is interesting, because in talking to Eddie Barefield, he also brought this up that, you know, talking about this style, that style. He says it was, you know --
It was just music. The bands that had formed didn't have organization until you had people like Don Redman, Fletcher Henderson to write for them. And the
struggling writers without the training that were making arrangements and whatnot because there were always arrangements, you know, somebody had an idea.
But to get it down to its final points, it's now. But now there aren't any of them.
(Laughter.)
Not too many of them, including me.
What was Stuff like to be with?
Stuff was --
To play with --

-- gorgeous, gorgeous. I loved playing with him. He -- I called him a pixie. He had a ball wherever he was, whenever, however. I remember Stuff had the band with Cozy and Jonah, and John Brown was on bass, and I forget who the piano player was at the time. And they were at the Green Room at the Edison Hotel.

And Stuff saw a chick pass that had a pretty voluptuous bottom, and he remarked about it. And somebody said, 'I dare you to touch it.' And he touched it with the bow. The band got fired if he didn't leave.
(Laughter.)
That's the kind of guy he was. Nothing bothered Stuff.
We were at the Garrett Bar in Chicago, and we'd follow Fats' small band. Fats had finished his engagement, and he's going on the road, and we come in -- we
came in for a short stay and stayed seven months. So my daughter was born while I was with Stuff. So that's a personal thing for me, my daughter.
And -- I lost the point --
You were telling about -- about his personality and about the band getting fired.
That was the Edison. Oh, we're at the Garrett Bar, yeah. And so the band was sensational. Herman Autrey was on trumpet. He just left Fats. Slick Jones had left Fats.
Oh, so they're playing with you.
Yeah. Yeah. And Sammy Benson was on the piano. And Joe Beders -- I don't know if you know that name -- he was a fine tenor player of that period. He was a tenor. That was our band with Stuff.
Was that his second name, or Joe was his first name?
Joe, yeah, Beders.
Beders.

Yeah. He was a half brother to Cass McCord, who was also a tenor player. And we worked seven days -- six -- seven days. This was before Chicago got five day a week, and we worked all around the clock. And everybody used to come down, FBI and -- we'd smoke pot with them.
(Laughter.)
The racetrack was there. So the jockeys used to come in, and Stuff -- oh, he's such a popular guy.

So let me backtrack a bit. When Stuff had Cozy and Jonah and Mack Walker, the bass player, and he had made 'Epes A-Muggin', which was a popular tune, and he was making a lot of money. So he was in Chicago, and he bought a LaSalle. That was a popular car then -- junior Cadillac.
And he drove it out of the showroom and wrecked it and went back and bought another one --
(Laughter.)
-- then went to California. So he hadn't been back to Chicago in a long time.
And people come up to the bandstand with requests, you know, written on a piece of paper. And this is a summons for that last LaSalle, and they garnished the whole band's salary.
(Laughter.)
So it was never dull with him.
No. So I guess our engagement was lengthened because we had to pay off the tab anyhow. My daughter was five months old when I came back, and she screamed, who's this character?
(Laughter.)
Now, Josh White was just as flamboyant
in his ways as Stuff Smith was in his way. They were opposite type of people. But it was quite an experience to work with him. I worked with him at the Cafe Society Downtown.
What was the instrumentation, yourself and him and that was it?
Just he and I on most of the recordings, but this was before we recorded, I made his first Decca -- 'Jelly, Jelly and One Meatball.'
'One Meatball,' yeah, that was such a big hit.

Yeah, I made those. And then I guess he changed record companies. I wasn't working with him steadily, you know, different periods of time. And then he went to Elektra records and made most of his Elektra records. Sometimes we had Sonny Greer. A couple times we had some extra musicians, basically just he and I. And we traveled and played colleges.

That's a funny one, the colleges we played. We -- am I getting lengthy? We had a date in Syracuse one winter, and we were supposed to leave at 10:00 o'clock in the morning to go to Syracuse. And this day it's snowing and sleeting like crazy, you know, and all the announcers are telling you, if you do have to drive, stay home and all this. But I got a record date with Bobby Hackett's band which I wouldn't

finish until 5:00.
So I told Josh, you go, and I'll get the train, and he immediately, you know, I'll make the job, you know hear. So Josh waited until I finished the day at 5:00, and we drove to make an 8:30 concert in Syracuse.
No way you could get there.

We weren't too far late, but we drove like crazy, and we were -- we had a bottle of vodka and orange juice chasers, and we'd alternate driving. And we plowed into that. We got to the concert just a little late, not too much, enough to go on. We didn't need any elaborate uniform, you know, any costumes, you know, shirt open to the belly button style.
(Laughter.)

So we got there. We played the concert. Then we were entertained after the concert, and we stayed up all night long because we got a concert at NYU the next night. And we stayed in Syracuse until 12:00. And the snow was still -- the highways were still snowy. And we got -- we got to the -- we got to the concert at NYU, and we just got a new fifth of Smirnoff, and the custodian saw us come in. He didn't know we were the act, you know, and he saw us come in with the bottle.
And we -- we needed this for survival, you see. We were just about making it. Well, with the confusion with
the bottle sort of delayed the concert a little bit. Then we went on.
What year was this?
In the '50s, I can't pinpoint. The incident just came up to my mind, so I can't pinpoint the year.
Well, I just wanted to put it in some kind of perspective.

In the '50s, yeah. So we played the concert. Meanwhile we're consuming the vodka. We played the concert, and Eddie Condon's was around on 3rd Street at that time. So it gives you sort of an idea how late it was or the period it was. And I finished the concert. I took my fiddle around to Eddie Condon's to leave it because I knew I couldn't handle it for the rest of the night, you know.
(Laughter.)
And we went our different ways, Josh and I. And the next day neither of us remembered doing the concert. Nor did I remember where my bass was.
(Laughter.)

That was the kind of traveling we did. Oh, we had some trips, just he and I, you know, and everybody -- Josh is going to give us a big party after a concert, and we've just come off the road all day, you know. And we went like that for a while.

He wanted me to go to Hawaii with him. He asked my parents when we were working out at Valley Forge in Philadelphia, and he was a houseguest, and he was trying to convince them that I should go to Hawaii with him, and I'm saying, no, for my own survival I'd rather stay here.
(Laughter.)
Do you find when you're working with an entertainer like, you know, a singer rather than a jazz group that you got more acceptance, you know, different levels of people?
Not necessarily.
No? I was thinking in terms of people sometimes are, you know, impressed more by personalities, you know, and singers certainly have this going rather than just the instrumentalists.

Well, working with singers, and I've worked with most of them, unlike playing in the -- in the band of instrumentalists -- he or she expects you to know each nuance, each gesture of their act, and any deviation from that, that's wrong.
Uh-huh. Well, I was talking about offstage, you know, just in traveling around.
Well, I haven't traveled around with many singers, no more than Josh. But I've traveled.
No, you've worked in New York mostly.
Yes, uh-huh.
(Side B.)

Professor, right? All right, Professor Ira Gitler, there are some names that -- some musicians that -- some of them, most of them are dead -- that should have been included in this creative period of music labeled jazz, and I'd like to name some of them -- Bill Coleman, Benny Morton, Mary Lou Williams -- she's had acclaim, but not as much as Marian McPartland. She's a creator.
Right.
Paul Webster, Freddie Webster -- they both worked with Jimmie Lunceford at different times. And do you remember Al Killian, the trumpeter?
Sure, I remember him with Jazz at the Philharmonic.

Yeah, that's right, uh-huh. Lips Page I worked with, Taft Jordan -- Taft was the swinging musician that -- of the period that I just started playing bass in Philadelphia when he was working with Doc Holder's band. And he was -- he was the trumpet player in Philadelphia during that period. That was the early '30s,
He modeled himself after Louis, didn't he?
Yes, all trumpet players did at that period, yeah. And then he left Doc Holder's in Philadelphia,

and he went with Chick Webb. So he was in New York before I got there. But we were on the same -- opposite bandstands. And Vic Dickinson, we -- he's one of the first musicians of note that I met while I was still in high school in Philadelphia, and he came through with the Blanche Callaway Orchestra.

So all of these -- all these musicians used to go to the Club Harlem after their shows, after their performances because that was the -- the heppest place in midtown near the hotel where they were staying. So I met Vic, and we've been friends ever since.

Eddie Barefield, yeah, Eddie and I've been associated for I don't know how long. We used to live near one another, and he'd have to pass where I was staying in order to get to the subway or whatever. And Tom Waley lived across the street, who was Duke's copyist, and Eddie Heywood lived in that building, and Pete Brown, the terrific alto man, was in that area.

And we used to -- and I was staying with a tenor player by the name of Lem Johnson. He and I lived together after I was separated from my first wife. And these guys would pass by the house -- Frankie Newton -- and we'd have jam session every day.
And then Flip started coming by, Flip -- Jazz at the Philharmonic --
Phillips.

Flip Phillips -- he's -- white musicians used to come uptown then. You know, it wasn't perilous for them. And we had a session going at all times, all hours, you know. That was our life. We had nothing else to do. We didn't have employment. That's for sure.
(Laughter.)
Yeah, but it seems, you know, even when there was employment, there were still jam sessions.
Oh, yeah.
It's just, you know, music was going all the time.

Well, that's how music was created, because there wasn't employment. So it's the same as a soldier with a gun. If he doesn't get to shoot it, he isn't much of a soldier, and an instrumentalist with an instrument doesn't get to play it isn't a musician, right?
Right, but the spirit of the jam session was always there, as I said, even when you were working, and you go and play someplace else.
Well, yeah, it was therapeutic, a release from what you did, you know. It wasn't a planned thing.
No.
It just happened. It was a happening rather than a planned thing.
Well, there were so many bands in those days too, so many people out there.
There were a lot of people out there, but there weren't too many bands.--
I'm talking about in the big band era.
-- working.

You know, in talking to Eddie Barefield, you know, he was saying kind of when you get to a city, this band would be there, that band would be there, and then, you know, people would -- sometimes he said they'd meet in the hotel lobby, and they'd start playing. Guys would get their instruments out and start playing.
True. True. But by the same token, they had to be traveling.
Yeah.
And, see, that -- I didn't experience too much of that.
No, you missed that, the glories and the horrors.
Mostly the horrors.
(Laughter.)
Wasn't too much glory. But this was a way of existence at that point.
What do you remember about Frankie Newton?

I thought he was a terrific trumpet player, and we were working opposite bandstands when I was with Billy Hicks. When I was with Billy Hicks, I worked opposite everybody, Tommy Dorsey, Benny Goodman, Chick, Erskine Hawkins, Les Brown, you know, everybody. We were the house group. So we had to fill in the time until they set up, got their instruments together.

But Frankie Newton, I think the last job I worked for him was at a place in the Village called the Little Casino. It was Stella Brooks. It was -- Frankie Newton was the leader, and Sammy Benskon was the pianist and me who worked there for a while.
And all the kids loved him in the Village. He was -- he was the king of the Village. He was giving lessons around, advice to the kids. That's when they would listen.
(Laughter.)
They would listen to an adult, I mean. And they loved Frankie.
He was considered somewhat of an intellectual, wasn't he?
Yes, he was very smart.
Well read?
Yeah, uh-huh. And great humanitarian. He gave of himself, not money because none of us were making any.
What other musicians do you have on
your list there?
I can't forget Don Redman. I used to -- we lived a block apart. I used to visit Don in the daytime, you know. We'd sit around and exchange stories and whatnot, another great humanitarian.
I've never met him, of course, but I've seen pictures of him, and he just seems to -- he kind of radiates something in those pictures.

Well, this was part of my education, you know. And he was -- he changed the style of the written jazz, you know, and he had a lot to do with that. And he went unheralded for so long, what he did and what we enjoyed and didn't realize that he was a part of.
Well, Eddie mentioned that Don could play any instrument in the band, and he'd seen him do it on occasions, you know.
Yes, and --
Somebody was missing in one section, you know, he'd just go up there and play the parts.

Right. I used to copy music for Luther Henderson and Sy Oliver and all those different people. And But Don -- and you'd get a score, and all the instruments would be in their various keys. The B flat tenor would be a tone higher. The alto player -- alto saxophone and the baritone saxophone would be a step and a half lower, and trombone would
be even with the original key, and then you have to transpose to this and transpose to that. And so hence a score for the composer.
But Don Redman could sit in the car and write out each part without the score in the proper key.
(Laughter.)
Jimmy Mundy could do that too. They'd sit in the back of the car and just write out the parts themselves, you know. They would hear it all.
Amazing. Who else do we have on that list?
Did I mention Happy's name (inaudible)?
Well, you did, but, you know, mention it again.
Well, Happy Caldwell is a member of my Masonic lodge.
I tried to contact him because he was working up at City College.
He was?
Yeah, in the custodial department, and I did speak to him when we were, you know, a couple years ago, but I don't know if he's still there. When is the last time you saw him?
I haven't seen him in a number of years, but I've talked to him on the phone.
Oh. Yeah, he was one of the earliest tenor saxophonists.
Yes, he's still blowing. Yeah. And Denzil Best.
Oh, yeah, I knew Denzil.
Denzil originally was a trumpet player.
I heard that, and then he had some -- trouble with his lungs?
Yeah, he had tuberculosis.
And so he --
And then he went to drums.
And he was such a talented writer.
Yeah, yeah. His things are heard now.
Yeah, all the time.

Yeah, and Red Allen -- let's see. Red had -- he was in Lou Russell's band. That's what it was -- at the Savoy Ballroom -- when I made my first legal record date with Red Allen and we did -- I think it was on Vocalian -- the Ritz Brothers, songs of their show, 'He Ain't Got Rhythm' and things like that. I forgot the titles of them because they were never too popular.
The Ritz Brothers.
Yeah. I mean the numbers weren't too popular.
Sing -- well, I remember a movie they
made. It was Sing, Baby, Sing, wasn't it?
I don't know the titles of the movies.
I remember that was one of the tunes. But that wasn't one of the ones you did.
No. And there were a lot of first recorders on there. Billy Kyle was one, and Honey Bear --
Gene Cedric.

Gene Cedric was on that date, and Harry -- you get old and doty all of them (inaudible) -- Harry Carney, he was playing baritone on the date. It's so long ago, you know, I can see the personnel and I think of the nicknames, and I can't recall their real names, you know.
The Golden Gate Quartet, I used to work with them a lot. Carl Kress and I used to record for them for Columbia.
With the Golden Gate Quartet?
With the Golden Gate Quartet, and Jimmy Crawford -- Jimmy Crawford on drums. We made most of their dates.
Were you on Stalin Wasn't Stalin' Alone?
Yeah.
That was quite a number for them at that time.
Yeah, that was a biggie. And a number of guys that I can think of -- I can't think of. I know, but

I -- you know, I can't recall the names. But there was a whole group of musicians that should have made it, and what brought this to mind was I went to the union the other day to get a record check, a residual from something that I did with Alberta Hunter, because every time they play a TV show, you're supposed to get a residual, whether it's in New York or -- but friends call me from elsewhere and tell me, you know, they've seen the show.
So I went there, and there was no check. When you do get a check, you're taxed at 1-1/2 percent out of that salary for the union.
The union takes 1-1/2 percent?

1-1/2 percent of all your earnings. So this -- this fellow was standing there with a stack of checks, and I hear the cashier tell him that his tax is $35.35 -- tax, -- $35.35. So I got to look at him, you know. Where is he working, you know? But he had them; even if it was a year's amount, I never paid $35.00 in tax.
That's a lot of work --
(Laughter.)
-- a lot of tax.

Well, man, if I had that much work, I wouldn't mind the tax. And I don't know -- and then the guys that can't even pay the rent, circa 1978, and they've contributed to the music as it is now, but they're not getting
any of the benefits, not even pensions.
No.
And the fellows are passing pretty fast, too. Oh, I didn't mention my best friend's name. May I? Jake Coleman -- do you know Jakie?
I know of him, just he was with Claude Thornhill --
Right.
-- and also he was on a Gil Evans' thing --
Yeah, for Columbia.
-- well, for Prestige and then for Columbia.
Yeah, he was with Little Jack Little's band in the earlier years.
But I don't know too much about his playing from hearing it, but from what I understand, he has a beautiful sound.
He plays a la Joe Thomas. Oh, Joe Thomas I didn't mention. Yeah, Joe Thomas. He plays similar to Joe Thomas, and that's quite neat within itself.
Yes.
But he's my closest friend.
He is, huh?
we're like brothers (Unintelligible).
Uh-huh, What is he doing now?

He's retired, He's retired now. His eyesight -- we were working in the theater for about ten years together, and he got something wrong with his eyes. His bifocals -- he'd have to have three sets of glasses, one to look at the conductor, one to look at the music and one to look at the -- whatever else he had to look at. And it became complicated, and he gave it up.
He's retired and --
Does he still play?
He plays. He plays gigs, yeah.

We had a beautiful gig out in Chicago, a friend of mine's 60th birthday, Pete Stern. He was one of the youngsters that came up in the early '40s and used to hang out at Jimmy Ryan's all the time. So he had me get the band, and I had Jake and Bud Johnson and George Masso, Cassius Fields was out there.
Really?

And Roy was a guest, Joe Jones was a guest. They were in the area at the time, And Ray Bryant was the pianist, and Dick Wellstood was the guest pianist.
All right. I handled that party for his 60th birthday in June, Yeah, it was neat.
(Laughter,)
Sitting there with GREAT musicians is like going to
a gourmet meal, you know. You don't know what to expect, but it's good.
(Laughter.)
One cookin' fine as the other.
Yeah. Yeah. He'll tell the secret ingredient.
Let everybody in on it.
Yeah. No, not everybody, just someone that understands.
Well, I mean most players.
Yeah,
Whoever can pick up.

Right. Right, it's there to -- and my present happiness is due to my best friend, Professor Fred Weinstein, who's been a professor at Yale and Southern Connecticut State College, and now he's writing a screen play. So that's what he's devoting his time to. But he was the best -- not only was he the best man. He introduced me to my wife.
(Laughter.)
So I'd like to have you meet him and his wife, Suzanne.
(End of proceedings as recorded.)
